How to Vet a US Research Peptide Supplier in 2026: A 12-Point Checklist

Six analytical checks, three compliance signals and three practical ones, each answerable from a supplier's public pages before you order

October 2, 2026·By Adam Reeves · Research Editor, Eppix Labs

In 2026 choosing a research peptide supplier stopped being only a question of price. The FDA sent warning letters to research-peptide websites and held a public advisory hearing on peptide compounding, and a lab that picked the wrong supplier put both its data and its supply at risk. This is the checklist we would use ourselves, written for that year. For the shorter nine-point version, see how to choose a peptide supplier in the US.

Eppix Labs supplies peptides for laboratory research use only. Nothing below is dosing, medical or legal guidance.

Key takeaways

  • ·In 2026, supplier choice is a research-quality decision and a continuity decision. A supplier that fails on testing undermines your data; one that fails on compliance can disappear overnight.
  • ·The FDA's March 2026 warning letters show what non-compliant sellers look like.[1][2][3] Use them as a negative checklist.
  • ·The strongest positive signal is batch-specific, independently verifiable analytical data covering identity, purity and content.

Part 1: Analytical quality

  • ·1. Batch-specific third-party certificates. Each lot should have its own report from an independent laboratory, with a batch number that matches your packaging. A single certificate reused across lots is not evidence about your vial. See how to read a Janoshik COA.
  • ·2. Independent verification. You should be able to confirm the report with the issuing laboratory, not only view a PDF on the seller's site.
  • ·3. Identity by mass spectrometry. HPLC purity tells you the main peak is dominant. Mass spectrometry tells you the main peak is the right molecule. This matters most for families of similar peptides, such as TB-500 variants or short bioregulator peptides.
  • ·4. Measured content, not just purity. A 99% pure vial can still be underfilled. Look for content measured against the label claim. See HPLC purity vs net peptide content.
  • ·5. A complete lot record. Ask what happens to batches that come back weaker than usual. A supplier that publishes every lot's result as the laboratory reported it, rather than only its best certificates, is giving you something testable.
  • ·6. Endotoxin data where relevant. For immune, inflammation and in vivo models, endotoxin is a major confound. See our endotoxin testing guide.

Part 2: Compliance signals

  • ·7. Real compound names. The FDA cited sellers who listed known drugs under coded names, such as "GLP-2 peptide" for tirzepatide.[1][2] A research supplier should name compounds properly and give sequence and molecular weight.
  • ·8. No human-use marketing. In the March 2026 letters the FDA cited outcome claims, human dosing schedules, and bacteriostatic water or syringes sold alongside peptides as evidence of drug intent.[1][2][3] Testimonials about personal results and before-and-after photos point the same way. Their absence is a good sign. Our research use only explainer covers the legal background.
  • ·9. Accurate regulatory content. Does the supplier describe the 2026 FDA actions accurately? Claims that a peptide is "FDA-approved" or "legal to compound" after the PCAC vote are a red flag for both accuracy and compliance. What the vote did is set out in the July 2026 PCAC vote.

Part 3: Logistics and support

  • ·10. Domestic shipping speed. Short domestic transit limits the time material spends outside controlled storage. Look for a named carrier, a stated delivery window and a clear daily cut-off for same-day dispatch. See lyophilized peptide shipping and storage.
  • ·11. Reachable support. Published hours and a real email address, with answers from people who can discuss batch data.
  • ·12. Clear pricing. Transparent per-vial pricing, stated volume discounts, and no surprise fees at checkout.

Scoring template

Score each criterion yes or no, with a note on where you found the answer:

  • ·1. Batch-specific third-party certificate
  • ·2. Independently verifiable
  • ·3. Mass-spec identity
  • ·4. Measured content reported
  • ·5. Every lot's result published
  • ·6. Endotoxin data available
  • ·7. Proper compound names
  • ·8. No human-use marketing
  • ·9. Accurate regulatory content
  • ·10. Fast domestic shipping with a stated cut-off
  • ·11. Reachable support
  • ·12. Transparent pricing

Frequently Asked

What is the single most important thing to check?

A batch-specific, independently verifiable certificate that matches your vial.

Are cheaper suppliers always worse?

Not always, but price cannot be judged without the analytical data. Compare cost per verified milligram.

Should I avoid suppliers that sell injection supplies?

The FDA has cited the sale of injection supplies alongside peptides as evidence of human-use intent. It is a meaningful compliance signal.

References

  2. US Food and Drug Administration, CDER (2026). Warning letter to Mile High Compounds LLC, MARCS-CMS 721600, March 31, 2026. Products listed under coded names, with dosing "cheat sheets" published through the seller's online community. FDA Warning Letters. Source
